projects.title: AI-Assisted Inventory of Speed Management Infrastructure on Washington’s Rural Roads
projects.sponsor: U.S. Department of Transportation / Washington State Department of Transportation
projects.detail: AI-assisted geospatial inventory of speed-management infrastructure in rural-to-town transition areas and rural community corridors.
projects.context: As co-principal investigator, I contribute to AI-assisted inventory methods for speed-management infrastructure on Washington’s rural corridors and approaches to towns. The work examines how imagery, available LiDAR and roadway records can identify treatments and locate them consistently. Detection, classification, spatial alignment and evidence review are separate tasks. The intended inventory supports corridor screening and the selection of sites for later evaluation with speed, crash and exposure data.

projects.title: Automated Active Transportation Facility Inventory for Rural Towns Using Computer Vision Techniques
projects.detail: Computer vision and GIS methods for identifying sidewalk and bicycle facilities from aerial imagery and maintaining geospatial inventories.
projects.context: I contribute computer-vision and GIS methods for identifying pedestrian and bicycle facilities from aerial imagery. The work connects feature recognition with network representation, including gaps, crossings and links to other facilities. Validation must consider location and connectivity as well as classification accuracy. The resulting research is intended to support repeatable inventory updates and the analysis of rural infrastructure coverage.

projects.title: Solution to Meet the Air Force Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Scheduling — Phase II
projects.sponsor: U.S. Department of Defense / U.S. Department of the Air Force
projects.detail: Optimization and AI-based decision support for strategic planning of humanitarian logistics operations.
projects.context: I contributed optimization and AI-based scheduling research for strategic humanitarian logistics planning. The work concerned coordination among service requirements, resource availability and scheduling decisions in time-sensitive operations. This project broadened my interest in allocation problems where the timing and continuity of essential services are central. My participation ran from December 2022 to May 2025.

projects.title: Selection of Level Crossings for Closure in the State of Florida: An Optimization-based Approach
projects.detail: Decision support for level-crossing closure selection, combining highway safety with freight-flow considerations.
projects.context: I contributed to optimization-based selection of highway–rail crossings for closure, considering safety, delay, maintenance, economic and environmental effects. My participation ran from June 2022 to June 2024. The completed FDOT project, contract BED30 977-04, produced a technical report and a decision-support application alongside related journal research. Subsequent collaborative work compares closure with grade separation and other countermeasures under multiple objectives.

researchStatement: Optimization and AI for coordinated, adaptive operations.
biography: I am a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus, working with Angela Kitali. My research lies at the intersection of operations research, artificial intelligence and operations and supply chain management. I develop mathematical models and algorithms for decisions whose consequences extend across operating stages, organizational boundaries and planning horizons.

I received my Ph.D. in Civil Engineering from Florida State University in August 2025 under the supervision of Maxim A. Dulebenets. My dissertation developed adaptive hyperheuristics for berth scheduling, combining algorithm selection with mathematical optimization. After continuing at Florida State University as a postdoctoral research scholar, I joined Washington in June 2026. I received my B.S. in Harbor, Waterway and Coastal Engineering from Wuhan University in June 2022.
homeResearch: My research examines how operations and supply chains can coordinate interdependent decisions and respond when operating conditions change. A schedule determines more than the use of one resource: it affects material availability, storage requirements and service commitments elsewhere. I study these dependencies through integrated scheduling, resource allocation and recovery models, with applications in distribution facilities, maritime logistics and infrastructure planning.

Methodologically, I develop mixed-integer formulations, decomposition algorithms and adaptive search methods that exploit the structure of an operating system. Published studies combine compact models with Benders decomposition and column generation, or use learning to select search operators alongside exact optimization. My developing interests in generative AI concern model construction, algorithm design and the use of solver feedback to revise analytical decisions.

My broader agenda connects supply chain coordination and resilience with electrification, automation and essential-service operations. I am interested in when better coordination can substitute for additional capacity, how flexibility should be prepared before disruptions, and how technology investments change operating choices. Healthcare, humanitarian logistics and public services extend these questions to settings where timeliness, continuity and access must be considered alongside efficiency.
academicContext: My training combines transportation engineering with operations research and computational optimization. After undergraduate study at Wuhan University, I pursued a Ph.D. at Florida State University, where my research focused on the mathematical and algorithmic structure of scheduling problems.

Working with Maxim A. Dulebenets, I developed hyperheuristic and hybrid optimization approaches for berth scheduling. Related studies extended to cross-docking, ship schedule recovery and infrastructure allocation. Together, these problems established my continuing interest in how modeling choices, adaptive computation and coordinated decisions affect operating performance.

I remained at Florida State University as a postdoctoral research scholar after completing my Ph.D. in August 2025. Since June 2026, I have worked with Angela Kitali at the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus. My current transportation projects concern AI-assisted infrastructure inventories, while my broader research examines optimization, supply chain coordination and the design of adaptive operating systems.

My project experience includes research supported by the U.S. Department of Defense, Florida Department of Transportation and U.S. Department of Transportation. I am a co-principal investigator on the Washington speed-management inventory project. My educational work includes graduate instruction in optimization and freight facilities, undergraduate and master’s research mentorship, and external master’s thesis committee service.

homeQuestions: How can models and algorithms coordinate decisions across an entire operating system?
How should plans adapt to changing demand, limited capacity and disruption?
How can AI assist optimization while keeping decisions mathematically valid and interpretable?

collaborationProfiles.title: Mathematical optimization and logistics
collaborationProfiles.text: My doctoral and postdoctoral research with Maxim A. Dulebenets developed formulations and algorithms for berth scheduling and cross-docking. This collaboration examines how compact models, decomposition and adaptive search can exploit operational structure, with published studies addressing both the design of solution methods and their computational performance.
collaborationProfiles.label: Compact models and decomposition

collaborationProfiles.title: Transportation infrastructure and public decisions
collaborationProfiles.people: Angela Kitali and University of Washington collaborators
collaborationProfiles.text: My work with Angela Kitali concerns infrastructure information for transportation analysis. I contribute to the speed-management inventory as co-PI and to computer-vision methods for pedestrian and bicycle facilities. These studies examine the relationship between automated feature detection, spatial data quality and the planning questions an inventory can support.
collaborationProfiles.label: CTIL research team

collaborationProfiles.title: Safety and resource allocation
collaborationProfiles.people: Ren Moses, Eren E. Ozguven, John Sobanjo and research coauthors
collaborationProfiles.text: Our highway-rail crossing research formulates closure selection as a resource-allocation problem with multiple consequences. The collaboration combines optimization with safety and infrastructure expertise to compare candidate choices and examine how input assumptions affect the resulting priorities.
collaborationProfiles.label: Rail-crossing decision study

collaborationProfiles.title: Adaptive algorithms and sustainable systems
collaborationProfiles.people: Marta Borowska-Stefańska, Szymon Wiśniewski, Yui-Yip Lau and research coauthors
collaborationProfiles.text: Joint publications address adaptive algorithms, maritime schedule recovery and sustainable supply chains. Across these studies, a shared interest is how computational methods represent interdependent decisions and expose trade-offs among operating objectives. Each publication provides the specific problem, contribution and complete author team.
